title: Ping-Pong was a trademark
hook: The sport is called table tennis because Ping-Pong was once a company's brand name.
peek: Around 1900, a London games firm registered the name Ping-Pong for its table-top tennis set. Rival makers and players had to find another name, and table tennis is the one that stuck for the sport.
lede: Tennis on a dining table was a Victorian parlour craze, played with books for nets and all sorts of homemade bats. Around 1900 the London games maker J. Jaques & Son registered Ping-Pong, after the sound of the ball, as its trademark. Other makers could not use it, so the sport's clubs and governing bodies settled on a plainer name: table tennis.

bullets.text: Before Ping-Pong caught on, the game went by names such as Gossima, an earlier Jaques product that sold poorly, and whiff-whaff. The arrival of light celluloid balls around 1900 made it far livelier.
Jaques sold the American rights to the name to Parker Brothers, the board game company. In the United States, Ping-Pong stayed a protected brand for decades.
In England a Table Tennis Association and a Ping-Pong Association both formed in the early 1900s. They later merged under the table tennis name.
When the International Table Tennis Federation was founded in 1926, the brand-free name was the obvious choice. In everyday speech, ping-pong never went away.
